papers.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang et al.
papers.summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

papers.title: PointX: Multi-View Consistent Intrinsics by Querying Surface Points
papers.authors: Miguel Farinha, Sam Sartor, Iliyan Georgiev, Giuseppe Vecchio et al.
papers.summary: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/

papers.title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
papers.authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman et al.
papers.summary: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

papers.title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
papers.authors: Yuwei Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Alejandro Lozano, Yuan-Sen Ting et al.
papers.summary: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.

papers.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
papers.authors: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano
papers.summary: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

papers.title: One Take, Many Cameras: Audio-Grounded Shot Synthesis for Dialogue Re-Cinematography
papers.authors: Anthony Chen, Naomi Ken Korem, Matan Ben-Yosef, Tavi Halperin et al.
papers.summary: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.

papers.title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
papers.authors: Zehan Zheng, Yanyuan Chen, Deming Li, Yutao Tang et al.
papers.summary: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

papers.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
papers.authors: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang, Wenbo Huang et al.
papers.summary: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

papers.title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
papers.authors: Xingjian Ran, Xiaoye Mo, Sihao Liu, Li Luo et al.
papers.summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

papers.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
papers.authors: Vansh Kapoor, Max Sobol Mark, Sreyas Venkataraman, Max Simchowitz et al.
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.

papers.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.authors: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li et al.
papers.summary: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce β-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.

papers.title: Neural Implicit Representation for Bathymetry Estimation using Sidescan Sonar Imagery
papers.authors: Tianxiang Lin, Sacchin Sundar, Fenghao Liu, Onur Bagoren et al.
papers.summary: Bathymetry measurement and estimation is critical for understanding the structure of underwater environments. While multibeam echosounders (MBES) provide accurate depth measurements, their deployment on surface vessels limits spatial resolution in deep water. Sidescan sonar (SSS), in contrast, can be deployed on autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to operate closer to the seafloor, enabling high-resolution acoustic imaging. However, the inherent ambiguity in measurements and the limited observation coverage of sonar datasets degrade the performance of state-of-the-art methods for underwater bathymetry estimation from SSS. In this paper, we propose a differentiable neural rendering framework for SSS that enables effective estimation of bathymetry from SSS measurements. Our approach incorporates a measurement model based on SSS geometry, explicitly accounting for its wide elevation aperture and associated ambiguities. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved robustness and accuracy compared to alternative approaches.

papers.title: Read My Lips: Context-aware Lip Reading Using Language and Audio-Visual Models
papers.authors: Amir Razlighi, Zhuo Ning, Naomi Ken Korem, Nisarg Patel et al.
papers.summary: Real-world speech is often partially observable: audio may be missing or corrupted by noise and competing speakers, while the speaker's lips remain visible. Recovering speech requires combining what can be heard, seen, and inferred from context. We introduce RML (Read My Lips), a collaborative method combining a lip reader, a language model, and an audio-visual generative model. The lip reader provides articulation hypotheses, the language model uses context to resolve ambiguous or missing words, and the audio-visual generator reconstructs synchronized speech while preserving speaker identity. Since source reliability varies, RML generates multiple reconstructions and uses the available evidence to favor the most reliable ones. This allows RML to handle missing audio, strong interference, and poor visual evidence without manually defined thresholds. Quantitative and qualitative experiments across these conditions show the benefit of combining visual, acoustic, and linguistic signals.

papers.title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
papers.authors: Karl El Hajal, Mathew Magimai. -Doss
papers.summary: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.

papers.title: A Bernstein-Type Variance-Adaptive PMW Mechanism for DP Query Release
papers.authors: Mohamed Aniss Benstaali, Habib Louafi, Naima Bessah
papers.summary: Private Multiplicative Weights (PMW) is a central mechanism for the differentially private release of adaptive linear statistics over a finite universe. Its classical analysis uses a fixed multiplicative-weights learning rate and does not exploit the local variance of the current hypothesis. This paper presents PMW-Bernstein, a variance-adaptive refinement in which the update step is determined by the relationship between the privately estimated query error and the variance under the current hypothesis. The mechanism retains the standard PMW privacy architecture based on Sparse Vector screening, Gaussian numerical measurements, sequential composition, and post-processing. Through a potential-based analysis, we prove a one-step progress bound that yields a global weighted energy bound, recovers the classical O(1/α2) update regime in general, and establishes an O(1/α) update regime under a Bernsteintype condition on updated rounds. Controlled simulations over synthetic finite-universe distributions and query workloads show that the adaptive rule reduces the number of updates in the low-variance regime, remains competitive in the high-variance regime, and succeeds within the prescribed update budget in the heterogeneous regime where the fixed-step baseline fails.

papers.title: Spectrify: Framework for Hyperspectral Image Generation Using Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Yasin Mamedov, Daniil Vladimirov, Sofiia Dorogova, Bakhtiyar Khalfin et al.
papers.summary: Hyperspectral images (HSIs) record the full spectrum of light at every pixel, so projecting an HSI through a camera's spectral sensitivities gives that camera's RAW image, and one HSI can supply training data for hyperspectral reconstruction and camera-pipeline methods. Real HSIs, however, are slow and expensive to capture, and the largest datasets hold only about 1,000 images. High-level vision commonly replaces scarce real data with images rendered from 3D scenes. Low-level tasks, however, need physically correct spectra, which requires spectral rendering with a measured spectrum for every material in a scene, and existing spectral renderings cover only a handful of scenes, mostly with a simplified image formation model. We present Spectrify, a framework that converts 3D scene datasets into HSIs, together with a library of reflectance spectra labeled by material and compiled from close-range hyperspectral datasets and spectrophotometer measurements. In Spectrify, spectra follow the material: each object receives a physically based optical model and measured reflectance spectra or optical constants from its material category, each lamp an emission spectrum of its type and the sky a modeled daylight spectrum, and Mitsuba 3 path-traces the full light transport of each scene per wavelength. We show that a hyperspectral reconstruction network trained only on our synthetic HSIs generalizes to unseen real datasets better than networks trained on the largest real HSI datasets on most test sets, and that assigning spectra by material category instead of by color alone improves this transfer on every test set. RAW images projected from our HSIs are also useful training data for color constancy, performing on par with existing synthetic RAW generators. We release the 4,500 rendered HSIs, the code of Spectrify and its material-labeled reflectance library.

papers.title: High-Performance Algorithms for Computing the V-BLAST Permutation
papers.authors: Tomer Pelleg, Haim Avron, Sivan Toledo
papers.summary: We propose two novel and efficient algorithms for computing a column permutation called V-BLAST or an approximation of it. The V-BLAST column permutation is used in a QR factorization that is part of an integer/discrete least-squares solver. The overall solver is part of the receiver in advanced communication systems that transmit multiple symbols simultaneously. Two classes of efficient algorithms for computing the exact V-BLAST permutation have been proposed in the literature. The first, based on a sequence of Givens rotations, is unfortunately highly sequential. The other, based on a sequence of downdating operations on a pseudo-inverse, has a shorter critical path, but is unlikely to be numerically stable. The new algorithms that we propose are inspired by the similarity between V-BLAST and rank-revealing QR factorizations. Our first algorithm uses Householder reflections, is numerically stable, and has a short critical path. It is unable, however, to efficiently exploit cache memories. We rectify this with a randomized algorithm that computes an approximation to the V-BLAST permutation and has a short critical path and can effectively exploit cache memories. We prove approximation properties of the randomized algorithm and demonstrate experimentally that both algorithms are faster than existing ones, both when tested in isolation and when tested within an integer least-squares solver.

papers.title: Blockchain-IoT Convergence for Spatiotemporal Data Systems: Challenges, Solutions, and Research Gaps
papers.authors: Natalia Chaudhry, Muhammad Murtaza Yousaf
papers.summary: Blockchain in conjunction with the Internet of Things (IoT) is changing the management of spatiotemporal data in a way that has never been possible before now. In the process of gathering geospatial and time-stamped data from a large network of IoT devices, data authenticity, accuracy, and timely processing are major issues. Spatiotemporal indexing in a blockchain environment is necessary for ensure quick data retrieval; supporting real time data processing requirement. Blockchain with its decentralized consensus mechanism is a possible solution for preventing data fabrication, unauthorized access, and single point of failure in IoT based spatiotemporal applications. This paper aims to describe how Blockchain and IoT indexing can be combined to enhance the spatiotemporal data management (specifically indexing and querying of data). Literature solutions will be reviewed and compared to highlight challenges and insights for future blockchain-integrated IoT in resilient spatiotemporal data ecosystems.

papers.title: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers
papers.authors: Zixu Zhou, Xiangyu Guo, Ilya Grishchenko, David Lie
papers.summary: Identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex translate authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. Due to their central role in authentication and trust mediation, a single vulnerability in a broker compromises every downstream service behind it. In fact, recent incidents have demonstrated that even widely adopted platforms are not immune to such issues, highlighting the critical need for systematic analysis. To build such an analysis, this work first defines invariants for broker operation. These invariants are not completely covered by existing authentication specifications, primarily because brokers are unique in their duality, i.e., acting simultaneously as a relying party and an identity provider. The invariants capture the properties that identity brokers must uphold throughout their workflows, as all 60 previous CVEs we consider violate at least one invariant. Within these workflows, we further define high-level action categories. Equipped with this information, our automated tool PORTA leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate API invocation sequences corresponding to the high-level action categories, and oracle assertions aligned with the specified invariants. PORTA identifies 33 previously unreported security vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers. We study these novel vulnerabilities and trace them to eight recurring patterns. We responsibly disclosed all discovered vulnerabilities: 29 have been confirmed, 14 patched, and 19 assigned CVE numbers, with 10 CVEs rated as critical.

papers.title: MESSI: Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration for Physics-Based Character Control
papers.authors: Xiaogang Peng, Jiaqi Zou, Lei Zhong, Sirui Xu et al.
papers.summary: Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

papers.title: Estimating GPU Roofline Arithmetic Intensity with Off-the-Shelf LLMs and Compiler Artifacts
papers.authors: Gregory Bolet, Giorgis Georgakoudis, Konstantinos Parasyris, Harshitha Menon et al.
papers.summary: GPU developers use profiling to understand computation and data movement, but access to target hardware can delay optimization. We investigate whether off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) can estimate Roofline arithmetic intensity (the ratio of floating-point operations (FLOPs) to device-memory bytes) without executing the target GPU workload. We evaluate three models (deepseek-v4-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gpt-5.6-sol) across 179 combinations of five kernel families, four NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, four parallel runtimes (CUDA, HIP, OpenMP, and OpenCL), and modified code variants, comparing source-only queries, queries with compiler artifacts, and sandboxed agentic analysis. Compiler artifacts raise the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within a factor of 1.20 of profiled values from 8-14% to 26-32%, while the resulting bandwidth-bound or compute-bound classifications are correct in 78-92% of runs. With compiler artifacts, FLOP estimates meet the 1.20x tolerance in 59-88% of runs, compared with 36-40% for device-memory traffic. Agentic analysis increases the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within the 1.20x tolerance by 6.5 percentage points for gpt-5.6-sol, at 3.6x the median cost and 2.5x the median latency of compiler-assisted queries; the other models incur higher costs without a statistically clear improvement. These findings suggest LLM estimates could help prioritize optimization when GPU access is constrained, while identifying cache-dependent device-memory traffic as the main obstacle to precise arithmetic-intensity prediction.

papers.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
papers.authors: Xingjian Wang, Shijian Wang, Minghao Liu, Ji Zou et al.
papers.summary: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.

papers.title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
papers.authors: Jie Li, Chenxu Niu, Tongyang Wang, Yong Chen
papers.summary: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

papers.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
papers.authors: Yi-Jun Chen, I-Tsen Hsieh, Li-Wun Chang
papers.summary: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.

papers.title: Mask-Based Speech Enhancement for Spatial Audio: Effects of Signal Representation and Channel-Specific Masking
papers.authors: Sheli Hendel, Boaz Rafaely, Dorothea Kolossa
papers.summary: Speech enhancement for spatial audio needs to improve speech quality and intelligibility while preserving the spatial characteristics of the acoustic scene. Time-frequency masking provides an effective approach for speech enhancement, but its performance and spatial fidelity may depend strongly on the signal representation in which the mask is applied. This work systematically compares time-frequency masking in the microphone, beamformer, and first-order Ambisonics domains in simulated reverberant acoustic scenes. Both an ideal ratio mask (IRM) and a lightweight deep-learning-based mask estimator are considered, with performance evaluated in terms of speech reconstruction, perceptual quality, intelligibility, reverberation preservation, and binaural spatial-cue preservation. The results show that channel-specific masking in the beamformer domain provides the highest speech quality and intelligibility, while channel-specific masking in the Ambisonics domain better preserves the spatial characteristics of the residual interference. Reducing the spatial representation from third- to first-order Ambisonics substantially reduces the performance gap between the beamformer and Ambisonics domains due to the lower spatial resolution of the resulting beamformers. Furthermore, a shared mask across first-order Ambisonics channels achieves speech enhancement performance close to that of channel-specific masking while requiring only a single mask-estimation network. These results demonstrate that the choice of signal representation and masking strategy should be considered jointly, and indicate that first-order Ambisonics with shared masking provides a practical compromise between speech enhancement performance, spatial fidelity, and computational complexity.

papers.title: KuroANN: Avoiding Unnecessary SSD Reads in High-Recall Filtered Vector Search
papers.authors: Soobin Cho, Nakyung Lee, Jiwoong Park, Gyuyeong Kim
papers.summary: We present KuroANN, a new on-SSD filtered vector search system for partition indexes. Existing solutions assign the same number of SSD reads to all queries within a given selectivity range, wasting I/O for many queries. KuroANN instead assigns each query's SSD reads based on the number of vectors that pass its filter, called its match count. This is based on our observation that the match count is known before the search and that the number of SSD reads a query requires depends on this match count. KuroANN measures offline how many partitions to probe and candidates to read for the target recall at each count. At runtime, a query looks up these numbers, filters only the probed partitions, and stops reading from the SSD when further reads are unlikely to help. This significantly avoids unnecessary SSD reads and filtering work, improving throughput and latency at high recall. Experimental results show that KuroANN outperforms PipeANN-Filter and Faiss by up to 34.5x and 9.10x, respectively.

papers.title: Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
papers.authors: Truong-Thanh Le, Hoang-Loc La, Amir Taherkordi, Frank Eliassen et al.
papers.summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) at the edge is increasingly desirable for privacy-sensitive applications and scenarios that require data to remain on local devices. However, edge environments are constrained by limited computational resources and exhibit substantial device heterogeneity, making efficient LLM serving challenging. These limitations become particularly pronounced under bursty demand, where congestion and queue buildup can significantly increase response latency. Replicating the model into multiple pipeline instances can improve serving capacity and reduce congestion. Yet, deciding how devices should be grouped into replicas, assigning replicas to prefill or decode functions, and partitioning model layers across heterogeneous devices jointly creates a large combinatorial optimization problem. We present Spade, a scalable and runtime-efficient placement planner for disaggregated LLM serving with pipeline replication across heterogeneous edge clusters. Spade introduces a dominance-based pruning technique that discards inferior replica candidates and recursively eliminates larger candidates that contain them, dramatically shrinking the search space. It further combines a water-filling approach for layer partitioning with a bounded multidimensional knapsack formulation that optimizes placement under a congestion-aware objective. On a synthetic fleet of 30 devices spanning five hardware classes, Spade finds the optimal placement in 441ms. In contrast, a genetic-search baseline augmented with dynamic-programming partitioning requires approximately two hours and still produces solutions with a 19.7% worse congestion objective. When evaluated on fleets containing ten device types, Spade's pruning strategy eliminates 99.6% of candidate placements while yielding the same surviving candidate set as exhaustive enumeration.

papers.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
papers.authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Antonio Anastasio Bruto da Costa, Alexios Lekidis, Pabitra Mitra et al.
papers.summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.

papers.title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts
papers.authors: Jian Li, Qinglin Zhao, Shuoyao Wang, Jincheng Cai et al.
papers.summary: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Prmpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Prmpt at ≥ 0.5) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Prmpt at =0.5, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. Code and data: https://github.com/Jamli58/fresh-keys-stale-secrets

papers.title: MSRGF: Multi-Source Reconstruction with Reference-Guided Fusion for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.authors: Yan Zhuang, Minhao Liu, Yanru Zhang, Li Ma et al.
papers.summary: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) predicts sentiment from textual, acoustic, and visual features when some observations are missing. Existing reconstruction methods estimate missing features from available modalities and combine the resulting information for sentiment prediction. However, different available modalities can produce distinct estimates of the same modality, while direct fusion often leaves the relationships among these estimates underused. We propose MSRGF (Multi-Source Reconstruction with Reference-Guided Fusion), which retains separate estimates and exploits their relationships during fusion. Specifically, MSRGF comprises three components: (1) Source-Wise Reconstruction (SWR), which uses modality-specific queries and a shared generator to produce a separate estimate of each modality from every available modality; (2) Reference-Guided Fusion (RGF), which uses relationships among estimates and available observations to construct a weighted reference, selectively refines it using their differences, and incorporates observed features when available; and (3) Global Context Modulation (GCM), which uses global context to adjust modality summaries for sentiment prediction. Extensive experiments on three datasets show that MSRGF outperforms existing methods, achieving average accuracy improvements of 1.9% on MOSEI under random within-modality missingness, 0.6% under random whole-modality missingness and 1.3% under fixed whole-modality missingness.

papers.title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
papers.authors: NaHyeon Park, Kyeong-Hwan Moon, Youjin Jeon, Hyunjung Shim
papers.summary: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.

papers.title: How Use Case Tables Enable the Elicitation of Explanation Needs
papers.authors: Lucas Burgath, Jovita Vahlhaus, Jakob Droste, Hannah Deters et al.
papers.summary: [Context and motivation] While software systems get more integrated into people's daily lives - like driver-assistance systems or smart-home applications - they are also becoming increasingly complex. When complex software is used, needs for explanations may arise. At present, explanation needs are usually elicited through the testing of prototypes or existing software. However, detailed documentation of software interactions, such as use case tables, might be a suitable alternative. Since use cases provide early insights into the key interactions within the system, they are appealing to employ as resources for explanation needs. [Question/problem] As of now, it remains unclear whether use cases allow the elicitation of explanation needs. Or, from a different perspective, whether their utilization for this purpose is desirable. [Principal ideas/results] We conducted a study in which users perused the description sections of use cases extracted from existing software. While reading through these use cases, they reported any explanation needs they encountered. Our findings indicate that use case steps are sufficient to induce explanation needs in the participants as they read the steps. [Contribution] This paper explores the novel idea of utilizing use cases for the elicitation of explanation needs and reports on a study that provides insights into the applicability of this concept with stakeholders.

papers.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.

papers.title: EviCraft: Can Minecraft Agents Find What They Cannot See?
papers.authors: Wenyou Yi, Lantian Zhang, Guanlin Chen, Xingqiu Xu et al.
papers.summary: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/AllenReder/EviCraft

papers.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Wonjune Seo, Minkyung Park, Saerom Park
papers.summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.

papers.title: Energy as a Service-Level Objective: Transaction-Level Energy Attribution
papers.authors: Julian Legler
papers.summary: Service engineers assess every change against functional requirements and qualities such as reliability, performance and availability. Energy is rarely part of this assessment. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.

papers.title: Cif-query bridging for audio-native asr transfer to visual speech recognition
papers.authors: Chang Sun, Dongliang Xie, Wanpeng Xie, Bo Qin et al.
papers.summary: Audio-native automatic speech recognition (ASR) models provide strong speech-language priors, but their compact acoustic interfaces are mismatched with long, frame-level visual features. We propose CIF-Query Bridge, a lightweight connection from a Paraformer visual speech recognition (VSR) encoder to Qwen3-ASR. The existing visual continuous integrate-and-fire (CIF) predictor produces an input-dependent number of token-rate queries; a two-layer cross-attention bridge refines them against the complete frame sequence, and a linear adapter feeds the pretrained ASR projector and decoder. This design preserves access to uncompressed visual context while avoiding direct autoregressive processing of hundreds of video frames. On CMLR, the complete visual-only transfer system achieves 7.97% character error rate, compared with 11.78% for native Paraformer under the same test split and scoring protocol—a 3.81-point absolute and 32.3% relative reduction. Controlled ablations characterize bridge depth, projector initialization, adapter capacity, and CTC supervision. The results show that CIF-derived adaptive queries provide a compact interface for transferring audio-native ASR capability to VSR.

papers.title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
papers.authors: Jan Robine, Marc Höftmann, Stefan Harmeling
papers.summary: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.

papers.title: AI-Generated Code Issues: A Taxonomy from Repository Histories, AI Conversations, and Developer Interviews
papers.authors: Rosalia Tufano, Nargiz Humbatova, Daniele Bifolco, Gunel Jahangirova et al.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate source code, yet the quality issues in such code remain only partially understood. Understanding these issues can help developers adapt quality assurance practices, such as code review and testing, to better detect problems that may be more common in AI-generated than in human-written code. We study how quality issues in AI-generated code manifest in real software development activities through a mixed-method empirical study that draws on evidence from three complementary sources. First, we mine GitHub commits whose messages explicitly attribute a fix to a problem in AI-generated code, and we manually inspect the 914 matched commits to remove false positives and classify the quality issue being corrected. Second, we collect developers' shared conversations with AI tools, identify conversations including source code and textual signals of model mistakes, and manually analyze 299 of them to classify the underlying quality issue. Third, we interview 20 practitioners and researchers who use AI coding tools to enrich and validate the obtained catalog of quality issues. From these analyses, we derive a taxonomy of 87 types of developer-attributed quality issues in AI-generated code, going beyond functional bugs. Our findings contribute an empirically grounded taxonomy and implications for the design and evaluation of AI coding assistants and agents.

papers.title: The Elephant-Goldfish Model for software design review: what a fresh reviewer can see
papers.authors: Sabry E. Farrag
papers.summary: A design can be easy to understand and still specify the wrong system. Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model asks fresh agents to review a design without the conversation that produced it. We examined how this choice affects detection of omissions, agreement violations and internal defects. We seeded nine defects in each of 47 public software design documents and supplied each with a scripted drafting conversation. A fresh reviewer given the conversation as its own earlier exchange detected 94.8% of omitted-decision instances, compared with 62.4% for the same model given the document alone. It detected 98.3% of violations of conversation-only requirements. On document-visible defects, recall was 87.5% with the conversation and 88.4% without it, equivalent within a prespecified 15-percentage-point margin. Three model judges scored detection and were calibrated on constructed controls. In document-only runs, the plugin's five-stage review took a geometric mean of 9.03 minutes against 1.81 for one reviewer. Its estimated recall was lower under both judging procedures, with a difference distinguishable from zero under one. A later generic-prompt comparison gave a similar result. The experiment separates two objectives for automated design review: testing whether a new reader can reconstruct the design and checking whether the design preserves the decisions that govern implementation.

papers.title: Lossless Re-Encoding of Vorbis and Opus Audio Files
papers.authors: Kamila Szewczyk
papers.summary: We present Balrogg, a lossless recompressor that replaces the entropy coding of Ogg Vorbis and Ogg Opus files with adaptive context mixing models. For Vorbis, we write each represent each codebook entry as a tuple of small signed integers (digits), binarized in five stages, and mixed with a direct context model, a bit-history model, and a match model, with weights selected by the neighboring digits and the previous residue pass. For Opus, each symbol is coded by an adaptive context model initialized with the codec's probability tables as priors, and the pyramid vector quantizer (PVQ) indices of the CELT layer are split recursively into pulse counts. At the default level, Balrogg reduces Vorbis music by 16.2%, Vorbis speech by 10.6%, and Opus speech by 5.4%; xz, zstd, ZPAQ, and bzip3 save at most 4.1% on the same files. Over 48 encoder configurations, files shrink to 66.5–96.1% of their size. Encoding and decoding are symmetric, run at 1.8–3.2 MB/s per core, and use less than 12 MiB of memory.

papers.title: Generating Property-Based Regression Tests from Source Code Semantics
papers.authors: Clemens Bauer, Johann Glock, Martin Pinzger
papers.summary: Conventional unit tests (CUTs) check a method under test at fixed concrete inputs. A test can therefore miss a regression if its input produces the expected output despite a fault. Property-based testing (PBT) checks universally quantified specifications across many randomly generated inputs, but writing properties and input generators by hand is difficult. Existing approaches automate PBT creation by generalizing an existing or generated unit test suite. They either over-approximate concrete inputs across repetitive tests or apply single-path symbolic analysis along concrete test runs. This paper presents an approach that derives property-based regression tests directly from source code semantics via multipath symbolic execution (SE). For each explored path through a target method, the approach records a path semantics comprising the path condition, the symbolic return value, and the state change map. Each path semantics induces a Hoare triple that compiles into an executable property. Because SE leaves parts of a class unspecified, the approach complements the generated properties with search-based CUTs for the whole class. We evaluate our Java implementation against EvoSuite and the test generalization tool Teralizer on EqBench and on 11 projects from TOGBench. On EqBench, our approach keeps validated properties for 82.0% of all methods. Its mean mutation score of 63.8% exceeds the 55.2% of EvoSuite and the 60.3% of Teralizer. On TOGBench, target selection, SE limitations, and property validation restrict validated properties to 2.8% of all methods. The resulting mean mutation score of 48.6% falls below the 50.9% of EvoSuite and the 51.1% of Teralizer. Failures during test generation leave a few classes without effective tests and lead to this gap.

papers.title: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
papers.authors: Kian Izadpanah, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Daniel Cohen-Or, Yiorgos Chrysanthou et al.
papers.summary: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

papers.title: Found in Translation: Five Entry Points to Translate AI Literacy Frameworks in the Design of Educational Materials
papers.authors: Luis Morales-Navarro, Karl-Emil K. Bilstrup, Mille Skovhus Lunding, Luke Connelly et al.
papers.summary: While there is a plethora of AI literacy and informatics frameworks, in practice it is difficult for designers of educational materials and educators to decide where to start and how to use these in learning activities. At the same time, recent reviews show that despite the fact that most frameworks emphasize the socio-technical nature of AI, in practice interventions tend to center on preparing learners to use AI. To address these issues, we ask: How can multiple stakeholders negotiate and translate AI literacy framework ideas into common language that can be used to design introductory learning materials for primary school children, teachers and parents? We introduce five entry points into AI literacy that were developed from a computational empowerment perspective through a participatory design process involving primary teacher educators, curricular designers, media producers, and researchers. We present three vignettes that illustrate how the entry points were generative in the design of learning activities, learning tools and media content for school and home. This paper contributes an account of the participatory development of five entry points that serve as generative and negotiable resources for designing educational materials.

papers.title: Protective-Design Pre-Emption in Child-Facing Generative AI
papers.authors: Verena Jasmin Hallitschke, Mahelie Dissanayake, Elisa Nguyen
papers.summary: Generative AI is adopted rapidly by children, yet unrestricted general-audience models dominate their usage. This paper presents the open problem of protective-design pre-emption: Delayed market introduction, low access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption foster unrestricted AI model lock-in, leading children to bypass child-centric platforms. With first signs of lower adoption of child-centric platforms, we argue that this shift may reinforce existing AI risks such as exposing children to deepened parasocial dependencies, skill erosion, and misinformation. To address this problem, we propose interdisciplinary research directions to quantify pre-emption, understand its socio-technical drivers, and develop interventions ensuring child-centric AI is actively adopted, not just available.

papers.title: Blaming the Machine, Billing the Victim? How Mock Jurors Reassign Fault from Generative AI Systems and Respond to Liability Cliffs in Tort
papers.authors: Tin Trung Nguyen, Jiannan Xu, Bao Kham Chau, Hal Daumé et al.
papers.summary: Generative AI complicates tort liability attribution when people blame a generative AI system that cannot itself bear legally relevant fault. We investigate where this blame goes when fault must be allocated among legal persons, and whether American discontinuous apportionment doctrines influence mock jurors' factual findings of fault. Such doctrines include Contributory negligence, Joint and several liability, and their 50% or 51% variations, all of which have a fault-percentage threshold or a "cliff" where the victim-entitled compensation (or a defendant's liability) jumps to zero (or to all compensatory damages). Our pre-registered human subjects experiment (N=199 Prolific participants) shows that as many U.S. mock jurors (36%) blame the AI system itself, the AI blame often "leaks" to the victim or to the AI user (in 27% to 73% of our AI-blaming records, depending on how leakage is calculated). Although mock jurors rarely change their blame assignment from one side of the liability cliff to the other, these participants do not acknowledge the legal doctrine or its monetary consequence when explaining their changes. Our empirical results illustrate how a narrow doctrinal exception in tort, carving out "joint and several liability" for those deploying or using Generative AI without reasonable care, might mitigate the impact of blame leakage on victims' deserved compensation without introducing significant jury nullification risks.

papers.title: MyMuse: A Personal Museum for Post-Visit Inquiry and Reflection
papers.authors: Jiyeon Bae, Chunggi Lee, Jinwook Seo, Hanspeter Pfister
papers.summary: Artwork photographs may preserve what visitors saw without preserving why it mattered. Revisiting them can involve recalling earlier responses and developing new questions and interpretations as knowledge and personal experiences change. Yet recurring interests may remain difficult to recognize across individual exchanges. Informed by a formative study with ten visitors, we present MyMuse, a post-visit system that connects inquiry about individual artworks with reflection across visitors' accumulated records. In its Personal Museum, visitors revisit artworks, ask questions, and record interpretations that inform subsequent system responses. Its interactive Narrative Report reorganizes the same records across artworks through four interpretive lenses. In two within-subject studies with 16 participants, direct comparisons favored MyMuse for vivid revisitation. The report received higher ratings for recurring-interest awareness, cross-artwork connections, and unexpected discovery than a per-artwork presentation of the same records. These findings suggest that examining accumulated records can support reflection on recurring interests and relationships among visitors' responses across artworks.

papers.title: CHORAL: A Multi-Agent Scaffold for Longitudinal Prognostic Reasoning from Patient-Generated Health Data
papers.authors: Youngji Koh, Esther Kang, Gyuna Kim, Seungwan Jin et al.
papers.summary: Longitudinal patient-generated health data can inform prognostic reasoning about how patients' conditions may evolve between follow-up visits. Existing approaches summarize trajectories or predict symptom states, but provide limited support for examining how heterogeneous evidence informs prognosis. We present CHORAL, a multi-agent scaffold that forms domain-specific appraisals before cross-domain synthesis and review, preserving evidence and revisions. Informed by a formative study with 12 psychiatrists, we evaluated CHORAL quantitatively and with 22 clinicians. CHORAL achieved balanced accuracy comparable to persistence (0.673 vs. 0.672), while detecting 40% of LOW-to-HIGH deterioration cases missed by persistence. Versus a single-agent baseline, it improved balanced accuracy from 0.639 to 0.673 and evidence coverage from 70.1% to 89.2%. Clinicians rated CHORAL significantly higher for evidence appraisal, alternative interpretations, grounds for challenge, and distinguishing what to rely on from what required verification. These findings show how multi-agent deliberation can support review by exposing alternative interpretations and grounds for verification.

papers.title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.authors: Jiaqi Yin, Baoyue Zhang, Jiyuan Zhang, Wenxuan Liu et al.
papers.summary: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/

papers.title: E-Waste-Bench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Visual Triage of Data-Center Hardware
papers.authors: Nader Lobandi, Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, Lombe Chileshe, Mohammad Mahoor
papers.summary: Retired data-center hardware can often be refurbished or resold, but triage demands more than object categories. A model must tell visually similar parts apart, judge condition under damage and occlusion, and read the printed part number. We audit nine public e-waste collections. They cover mostly consumer devices (only 10% of images are labeled as a data-center part), label neither condition nor printed text, and contain 42% exact or augmented duplicates. We introduce E-Waste-Bench, 328K photographs drawn from 762K deduplicated images and labeled for class (24 classes), granularity, condition and printed text. Images come from those collections and the web, where a recipe-based crawler works beside an agent built on an open-weight vision-language model. The agent vets new sources and reads sites the crawler cannot parse, and both are steered toward under-represented classes. Training labels are model-made, splits follow near-duplicate groups, and human annotators label a test set of nearly 10,000 images. We benchmark classification, condition, detection, text perception and cross-dataset transfer. On this test set, a ConvNeXt-T trained on E-Waste-Bench reaches 64.3% top-1, against 31.5% with the public collections alone. Near-duplicate leakage inflates top-1 by 3.0 points under model-made test labels but by less than 0.1 under human labels, so model-labeled benchmarks need group splits. Accuracy falls to 42.1% on marketplace and auction photographs, the closest proxy for hardware leaving service. Data and code will be released.

papers.title: CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence
papers.authors: Erik Derner
papers.summary: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another.
